newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: FEATURE-Brutal murder sows fear in Argentine media.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Brutal murder sows fear in Argentine media.

text.p: When police found the body of Jose Luis Cabezas in the beach resort of Pinamar, it was so badly burned it could be identified only by the Argentine news photographer's car keys and wristwatch.

The assassins of the 35-year-old father of three handcuffed and tortured him, shot him in the head, doused him with fuel and set him ablaze in late January. Police are still probing whether this most brutal attack on the news media since the end of military rule was a personal vendetta or was intended to stop Cabezas' prying camera for good.

It has been followed by daily threats to journalists and is interpreted by many in Argentina's aggressive media as a clear warning not to delve too deeply into foul play. The murder has galvanised journalists and fired the anger of many Argentines who vividly recall death squad massacres that terrorised the nation during 1976-83 military rule.

"Cabezas reminds me of the face of many of the children who disappeared," Jacobo Timerman, a former newspaper editor who was tortured by the junta, wrote recently. "The greatest danger is for this to pass, because people do forget horror."

The photographer was covering the holiday season in Pinamar, a favourite of the rich and powerful, for Noticias news magazine. The top-selling weekly has uncovered corruption scandals and has been highly critical of President Carlos Menem's administration.
Cabezas took part in investigations into graft in the police and mafias allegedly run by a top businessman.
GOVERNMENT RULES OUT NOTHING
Interior Minister Carlos Corach, asked whether the murder could be politically motivated, said, "I don't rule out any hypothesis, including the one you mention."
A recent poll showed 85 percent of Argentines thought the killers "have links with political powers" and 59 percent felt it "presages a new wave of political violence."

Five suspects are being held, including a woman who is a convicted killer and drug dealer and goes by the alias "Pepita the Gunslinger." But investigators do not consider any of them to be the mastermind behind the killing. They are also probing some Buenos Aires Provincial Police members in the case.

Leaflets reading "Don't forget Cabezas" have become a common site in Buenos Aires and many reporters, photographers and television anchors now wear black mourning ribbons. A recent rally outside the Noticias offices to demand justice attracted thousands including politicians, unionists and human rights activists. Taxis and buses stopped and church bells tolled.

"For those of us privileged to be close to the centre-point of the Noticias magazine offices, the mixture of tragedy and of fear brought the specter of the past," Andrew Graham-Yooll, editor-in-chief of the Buenos Aires Herald, wrote in an editorial. "Who, of a certain age, cannot remember the charred bodies in burned-out cars on the road to Ezeiza airport in the '70s? And there, as a mirror of misery, is the picture of Cabeza's car, nearly reduced to ashes."
PAYING SILENT HOMAGE

The outrage has spilled outside the media community. Both houses of Argentina's Congress met jointly for the first time since 1987 to declare their grave concern. Authorities are offering a $300,000 reward for clues leading to the killers. And minutes of silent homage have been observed by such unlikely sympathisers as soccer clubs, the military and truck drivers.

The Union of Buenos Aires Press Workers (Utpba) reports 720 "intimidating" acts against journalists from 1989 until the Cabezas killing, including telephone threats, physical assaults and lawsuits. But since the Cabezas murder on Jan. 25, there has been an average of one threat per day.

"It is not logical to assume that all these cases are isolated. There is an organisation dedicated to fostering censure," Jorge Goldemberg, the union's human rights secretary, said. "They want to send a message that we cannot report dirty dealings."

The press is particularly worried in light of Argentina's bloody past. The Utpba reports that 103 journalists, many of Argentina's finest, "disappeared" or were known to have been killed during the dictatorship.

"We feel that the freedom of the press has been seriously compromised," the Argentine journalists' lobby ADEPA said in a statement. "It is the worst case affecting the Argentine press since democracy was restored in 1983."

Leading newspaper columnist and television commentator Joaquin Morales Sola says the news media has been very aggressive and left various sectors of society resentful. "There is a lot of fear," he told Reuters. "It has left open the possibility that any of the threats could be serious.
"It is not clear whether this (intimidation of the press) begins or ends with Cabezas. We have to ask whether it will end with us censoring ourselves out of fear for our safety."
